title: Count the Beautiful Arrangements
statement:
An arrangement of the numbers `1` to `n` (each used once, positions numbered from `1`) is **beautiful** if for **every position** `i` the number `p` placed there satisfies at least one of: `p` is divisible by `i`, or `i` is divisible by `p`.

Return the number of beautiful arrangements.

examples.explanation: Eight of the 24 arrangements of 1..4 fit the rule.

hints.nudge: Fill the positions from 1 upwards (or from n downwards). For a position, only a few numbers fit. Why is it a waste to build a whole arrangement before checking it?
hints.pattern: Backtracking: place a number in position i only if it satisfies the rule and has not been used; undo and try the next one. The count of ways depends only on WHICH numbers are used (a bitmask), so the search can also be written as a dynamic programme over bitmasks.
hints.pseudocode:
go(pos, usedMask): if pos > n: return 1
  total = 0; for num in 1 .. n: if num not used and (num mod pos == 0 or pos mod num == 0): total += go(pos + 1, usedMask with num)
  return total
hints.walkthrough: All n! arrangements checked one by one is too slow for n = 12 (479 million). Placing numbers position by position and testing the rule at once cuts most of them before they are complete (position 1 accepts every number, but position 7 only accepts 1, 7 and a few others). That is plain backtracking and handles n = 12 quickly. The number of ways to complete the arrangement depends only on the position reached and on which numbers are used, so you can also number the used-sets as bitmasks: dp[mask] = number of ways to fill positions 1..popcount(mask) with the numbers of the mask. Both approaches are fast for n up to 12.
